title: What Does Weight-Space Programming Add to Diffusion Editing? Program Construction versus Score-Guided Refinement

target_networks.name: Stable Diffusion v1.4 (cross-attention K/V projections, 32 matrices)

headline_result.text: One-shot Astra programs raised fresh-scene VLM joint success by +10.0 points over a shared-panel hand-written baseline, but score-guided rewriting raised CLIP by +6.2 while joint success fell by 9.7, and the preregistered rewrite pipeline showed no advantage.
headline_result.quote: Figure 1. Astra’s construction gain is lost after score-guided rewriting, even as CLIP rises.

evidence_quality.n_runs_or_seeds: one program per edit and model; 12 image seeds per prompt

key_claims.claim: The preregistered primary method (Opus probe-and-rewrite) showed no advantage over the strong hand-written baseline.

key_claims.claim: In an exploratory contrast, one-shot Astra programs improved fresh-scene joint success by about 10 points with no detectable CLIP difference.

limitations_stated.text: The component transplant tested a different (two-sided) variant than registered, so the program's gain remains unattributed.
limitations_stated.quote: The image-level results reported here belong to the two-sided variant; the input-only transplant remains unevaluated.

notes_for_review: A careful, partly preregistered comparison of LLM-written weight-update programs for Stable Diffusion concept editing against published closed-form editors, a hand-written baseline using the same fitter, and budget-matched random search. The preregistered claim is null; the positive Astra one-shot result is exploratory and does not survive full Holm correction. Its main contribution for the review is evidence that score-guided LLM revision optimises the proxy (CLIP) while losing task value, a Goodhart-type failure, and that the numerical fitter and LLM-proposed protection panels are confounds shared with baselines. Only 24 of 104 TIMED edits; code and artifacts promised but not yet released.
